arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: General Bullock argued that the compact freezes total water consumption.
Justice Roberts noted that beneficial use is irrigation and questioned if usage increased after diversion.
Justice Sotomayor asked if pre-1950 irrigators could change their crops.
Justice Kennedy suggested the compact language might only show reduced water amounts.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Montana and Wyoming argue over the meaning of a 1945 interstate compact. The states disagree on whether the agreement freezes total water consumption or only the amount diverted from the river. This distinction determines how much water each state may use for irrigation.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on January 10, 2011.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Montana wants the Court to interpret the compact as freezing total water consumption.
Wyoming wants the Court to interpret the compact as freezing only the amount of water diverted.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Montana argues that the compact limits the total volume of water a state can use.
Wyoming argues that the compact limits only the physical amount of water taken from the river.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Ginsburg asked for the specific language that freezes consumption rather than diversion.
Justice Kennedy asked why Article V(A) does not simply restate the beneficial use issue.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The interpretation determines the total volume of water available for agricultural irrigation in the basin. It defines the legal boundary between diversion limits and consumption caps for upstream and downstream states.
